context.title: Unpaid Internship
body: Summer internships allow students to enter a workplace before they make long-term career choices. A company may offer an unpaid placement in which an intern observes meetings, assists with simple projects and learns how staff communicate with customers. The experience can help a young person test an interest, collect examples for a future application and understand why punctuality, accuracy and teamwork matter.

However, an unpaid intern still gives time and effort. Transport and meal costs may make the placement difficult for students from less wealthy families. Some interns receive useful guidance, while others are asked to repeat routine tasks without proper training. Long working hours can also affect rest, study plans or a summer job that would provide income.

A worthwhile programme should therefore state the hours, duties, supervision and learning goals clearly. Schools could help students check whether a placement is safe and relevant. Interns should be curious, dependable and willing to ask questions, but employers should also provide feedback and treat them respectfully. The value of an internship depends not only on its name, but on what the student is genuinely allowed to learn.

context.title: Mooncakes and Mid-Autumn Festival
body: Mooncakes remain a familiar part of Mid-Autumn Festival in Hong Kong. Families, friends and businesses give them as symbols of reunion and goodwill. Yet a household may receive more boxes than it can eat, and elaborate tins, plastic trays and paper bags can create a large amount of waste after a short celebration.

Traditional lotus-seed-paste mooncakes carry cultural meaning, but many consumers now choose smaller portions, reduced-sugar recipes, ice-cream flavours or products made without animal ingredients. New versions may attract younger customers and people with different dietary needs. At the same time, replacing every traditional product could weaken a custom that connects generations.

The festival can be celebrated without treating gift-giving as a competition. Shops could offer simple packaging, allow customers to return boxes or sell mooncakes individually. Families might share one box, donate unopened products early, reuse lanterns and avoid disposable glow sticks. A balanced approach would preserve the meaning of the festival while reducing unnecessary food and packaging. The most valuable gift may be time spent together rather than the size or price of a box.

context.title: Cosplay
body: Cosplay involves dressing and performing as a character from animation, comics, games or films. In Hong Kong, participants meet at conventions, shopping centres and photo events. Some design costumes by hand, learn make-up techniques and practise poses or short performances. Online communities also allow beginners to share work and find advice.

Supporters see cosplay as a creative hobby that combines art, craft and drama. It can help shy people meet others with similar interests and express a side of their identity that is not visible at school or work. Critics may consider it childish, expensive or too focused on appearance. Public misunderstanding can make cosplayers uncomfortable, especially when photographs are taken without permission.

Experienced cosplayers can make the community safer and more welcoming. They can explain event rules, teach low-cost costume methods and remind newcomers about consent, copyright and suitable public behaviour. Organisers can provide changing areas and clear photography guidelines. Whether cosplay becomes more widely accepted will depend on how participants present their hobby and how respectfully the public responds to forms of creativity that may look unusual at first.

context.title: Stephen Chow Project
body: A school film club is planning a Stephen Chow festival to introduce students to an important figure in Hong Kong popular culture. Chow began as a television performer and later became known for a distinctive form of comedy that mixes wordplay, physical action and unlikely heroes. His development from actor to writer, director and producer gives the club several possible themes.

Students could research his early career, major films, comic style and influence on audiences in Hong Kong and overseas. Useful sources might include recorded interviews, film reviews, library archives and comments from people who worked in the local film industry. Information from fan sites should be checked against more reliable sources before it is used.

The festival could combine screenings with short introductions, a poster exhibition and a discussion about how comedy can communicate serious ideas. Students might recreate a scene, compare subtitles or vote for a film to show. The programme should not become a simple celebration of fame: it should help the audience understand how film-making choices, local language and changing social conditions shaped Chow’s work and its lasting popularity.

context.title: Technological Products
body: New technological products appear quickly in homes, schools and workplaces. People are attracted by devices that save time, provide entertainment or make communication easier. A smartphone can combine a camera, map, payment system and learning tool, while smart appliances can perform routine tasks with little effort from the user.

These products can improve access to information and support people with particular needs. Video calls connect distant relatives, translation tools reduce language barriers and health devices can remind users to exercise. However, a product is not automatically useful because it is new. Some devices are expensive, difficult to repair or designed for a problem that could be solved more simply.

There are also questions about privacy, electronic waste and dependence. If a service stops working, users may lose access to important information or basic functions. Before buying a product, consumers should consider its real purpose, expected life, energy use and the support offered by the company. The best technology is not always the most advanced one; it is the product that meets a genuine need without creating unnecessary cost or harm.

context.title: Keeping a Diary
body: Keeping a diary gives people a private place to record events, thoughts and feelings. A short entry can preserve details that might otherwise disappear, such as a conversation, a small success or a difficult decision. Looking back later may help a writer notice changes in habits, relationships and personal goals.

A diary does not have to be a formal daily essay. Writers can include photographs, sketches, tickets, lists or a few sentences about the most memorable moment of the day. Some prefer paper because it feels personal and has no notifications. Others use a password-protected digital diary because it is searchable and can include audio or images.

The habit is easier to continue when expectations are realistic. A writer might choose a regular time, use prompts and accept that some days will be missed. Privacy also matters: paper diaries need a safe place, while online accounts need strong passwords and careful backup settings. A school campaign promoting diary writing should present it as a flexible tool for reflection and creativity, not another piece of homework that must be perfect.

context.title: Swimming Across Victoria Harbour
body: Hong Kong’s cross-harbour swimming race returned after a long break, with competitors travelling from the Lei Yue Mun side towards Quarry Bay. Applicants had to show that they could complete a qualifying swim within a set time. Organisers limited the number of places and planned support boats, medical teams and a route separated from normal marine traffic.

Swimming is a popular form of exercise in public pools and at beaches, but an open-water race creates different risks. Currents can carry swimmers away from the route, and weather, tiredness or poor visibility can make rescue more difficult. Water quality must be checked because competitors may accidentally swallow polluted water. Even experienced pool swimmers need preparation for waves and close contact with other participants.

If managed safely, the race can offer a demanding personal goal, revive a local sporting tradition and draw attention to the harbour environment. It may also attract visitors and encourage more people to learn swimming. Whether it should become an annual event depends on safety records, environmental conditions and the organisers’ ability to protect both competitors and other harbour users.

context.title: Study Tours
body: A proposed summer study tour would place Hong Kong students with host families in Oxford. Weekday mornings would include intensive English classes, while afternoons would be divided between sports, local activities and visits to historic places. The real challenge is not only finding more space, but ensuring that limited space is designed and distributed in a way that supports a reasonable quality of life.

context.title: 3D Movies
body: Three-dimensional films use separate images for each eye to create an impression of depth. Improved projectors and successful action and animated films have made the format more visible in Hong Kong cinemas. For some viewers, objects appearing to move towards the audience make a film feel more exciting and turn a cinema visit into a special event.

Too many distractions may make an audience notice the technology instead of the film. The decision to use 3D should therefore be made by considering the genre, artistic purpose, cost and comfort of viewers rather than assuming that every new film needs the same treatment.

body: Old buildings can show how people in Hong Kong once lived, worked and travelled. Their materials, signs and layout may preserve details that photographs cannot fully communicate. Not every old building can be preserved, but development should not erase valuable heritage simply because rebuilding is faster or more profitable.

body: Chinese white dolphins live in waters affected by shipping, construction, pollution and fishing activity. Environmental groups, businesses and government must also report whether measures work. Conservation is strongest when decisions are based on long-term evidence and when the public can see how protecting dolphins also supports the wider marine ecosystem.

context.title: Money Management Skills
body: Good money management involves more than saving every dollar. Young people need to understand how money is earned, how to separate needs from wants and how small choices affect a budget. They should also learn that spending, saving and donating can all be reasonable when they are planned responsibly.

A cartoon can introduce these ideas through characters and everyday situations, but watching alone may not change behaviour. Students learn more when they make decisions themselves. A class could plan a meal with a fixed budget, compare prices, divide imaginary income among several goals or discuss how advertising creates pressure to buy.

Activities should reflect real life without asking students to reveal private family finances. Schools might use games, a savings challenge or a small charity project, followed by reflection on the choices made. Digital payment should be included because cashless spending can make costs less visible. The purpose is not to tell everyone to make identical choices. It is to help students ask useful questions, recognise risk and make decisions they can explain before financial mistakes become difficult to correct.

context.title: Restaurant Reviews
body: Hong Kong restaurants offer food from many regions, from Cantonese dim sum and regional Chinese dishes to Japanese, South-East Asian and European cuisines. This variety gives reviewers many choices, but it also means that a fair review should understand what a restaurant is trying to provide rather than compare every place by the same standard.

A good restaurant usually combines fresh, well-prepared food with cleanliness, reasonable value and service that suits the setting. Decoration may shape the atmosphere, but an attractive room cannot make up for unsafe food or rude treatment. Reviewers should consider portion size, menu information, waiting time and whether dietary needs are handled clearly.

A useful review identifies the restaurant, location, price range and dishes ordered. It separates observation from personal preference and gives specific examples instead of simply calling the food “good” or “bad”. Reviewers should also disclose invitations or free meals and avoid judging an entire business from one minor mistake. Honest criticism can help customers choose and restaurants improve, provided it is accurate, balanced and respectful to the people whose work is being discussed.

body: Reality shows place ordinary people, performers or celebrities in competitions and unscripted situations. Younger audiences may follow contestants online, while older viewers may prefer programmes that demonstrate skill or tell a clear personal story.

context.title: English Lessons with Video Games
body: English lessons can be memorable when students use the language for a clear purpose. Role-plays, songs, debates and collaborative tasks may feel more meaningful than completing isolated exercises. Games can enrich an English lesson, but they work best as one carefully guided method among many rather than a replacement for explanation, reading, discussion and feedback.

body: Home swapping allows two households to stay in each other’s homes during the same period. Travellers may avoid hotel costs and live in a residential area with a kitchen, neighbours and ordinary local services. This can provide a closer view of daily culture than visiting only tourist attractions.

The arrangement also involves trust. Property may be damaged, personal belongings can be exposed and expectations about cleaning, pets or the use of equipment may differ. A safer exchange needs verified identities, honest descriptions, written house rules and a clear plan for emergencies. Participants should agree on dates, guests, keys, expenses and what happens if either side cancels. Reviews can help, but direct conversation is still important. Home swapping may offer value and cultural contact for some travellers, yet it is not automatically more authentic than a hotel stay. The experience depends on preparation, mutual respect and realistic expectations.

body: Traditional toys and games such as kites, marbles, skipping ropes and board games remain part of childhood memories in Hong Kong. The most successful toys will not necessarily use the most technology. Parents and children may continue to value durability, imagination, safety and the ability to play together. A project on toy trends should therefore compare what different forms of play allow children to do, rather than simply treating old toys as outdated and new ones as better.

Building transferable skills and learning how to reassess goals may be more useful than searching for one perfect job.

context.title: Outdoor Music Festivals
body: Outdoor music festivals are major cultural and commercial events in some cities, but Hong Kong has limited open space and many venues are close to homes. Organisers argue that audiences want to hear pop, jazz, independent music and other performances outdoors. Residents may worry about sound tests, late-night noise, crowds and transport disruption.

A festival can support local musicians, attract visitors and create a shared public experience. It can also fail if the site is too small, weather plans are weak or ticket prices exclude much of the community. The West Kowloon Cultural District could use clear finishing times, sound monitoring, transport plans and advance notices to nearby residents. Other suitable events might include open-air theatre, dance, film, Chinese opera or community arts days. Decisions should consider artistic value, public access and the impact on the neighbourhood. A successful festival needs a space designed for performance and rules that allow culture and everyday life to coexist.

context.title: Plastic Surgery for Men
body: Plastic surgery is increasingly marketed to men as a way to change facial features, body shape or signs of ageing. Some clients seek treatment after injury or because a physical feature causes serious distress. Others believe appearance affects confidence, relationships or career opportunities. Advertising and images of male celebrities may make procedures seem more ordinary than before.

Surgery can produce the desired result, but it also carries medical risks, pain, recovery time and cost. Expectations may be unrealistic, and a person who remains dissatisfied could seek repeated procedures. Social pressure is especially concerning when people feel they must look a certain way to be accepted. Non-surgical treatments are not automatically risk-free either.

Anyone considering a procedure should receive independent medical advice, understand alternatives and check the qualifications of the practitioner. Clinics should explain complications honestly rather than promise perfect results. Men deserve the same freedom as women to make informed choices about their bodies, but rising popularity should not prevent careful discussion of health, self-image and commercial influence. Confidence may improve through surgery, yet appearance is only one part of a person’s well-being.

context.title: Memory Training
body: Memory supports learning, work and everyday independence. Remembering instructions, names and appointments can save time and build confidence. Students may benefit when they can connect new information with what they already know, while older adults may value strategies that help them manage daily routines.

Memory can be trained through active recall, spaced review, association and organising information into meaningful groups. Sleep, exercise and focused attention also affect how well information is stored. Repeating words without understanding may help for a short test but is less useful than explaining ideas, applying them and reviewing them over time.

Different people need different methods. A musician may remember sound patterns, a professional may use checklists and a student may create diagrams or practise questions. Training should not promise impossible results or suggest that forgetting is always a personal failure. Phones and reminders can support memory, but complete dependence on them may weaken attention to important details. A good programme combines practical techniques with realistic goals and recognises that judgement and creativity remain important even when facts can be remembered accurately.
